title: Multi-Day Trek Roadbook: Day-by-Day Plan
description: Route a trek and split it into days with the Multi-Day Trek Roadbook — leg table, day-by-day split and the place each day ends. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 46-mile trail split over four days becomes four legs of roughly 11–12 miles with a named place near each day's end — an itinerary you can carry on paper.
quick_answer: The Multi-Day Trek Roadbook routes your trek from start through waypoints to the finish, divides total distance across your chosen number of days, and lays out a leg table and a day-by-day split with the place each day ends near — a document built to be printed and carried.

Everyone carries the same roadbook: the day's distance, the day's end. Disputes about 'not far now' end at the trailhead.
The day-end places are the support driver's itinerary too — where to meet, where to hand over luggage, where the spare socks are.
Phones die in mountains; roadbooks do not. The printable document is the trek's analogue insurance.
46 miles over 4 days ≈ 11.5 miles a day. The roadbook names the country near each day's end — the difference between an itinerary and a hope.
Real treks are not metronomes: a short day before the big climb is planning, not weakness. Set the days, read the split, and adjust waypoints until the days match the walkers.

faq: How are the days divided?
The routed distance is split across your chosen day count, and the roadbook reports where each day's share ends — the place near that point becomes the day's named ending.
Can I save it offline?
Yes — the roadbook is built to print or save, and paper works where signal does not. That is rather the point of it.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Trails have weather and daylight instead of traffic; the planner divides distance, and your judgement divides the days further if conditions demand.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Trails wind longest of all. The roadbook divides the routed distance — the ground your boots will actually cover.
Can route results change over time?
Paths are re-routed and huts close; rebuild the roadbook for each season's trek rather than trusting last year's printout.
Can days be uneven?
The split starts even and the waypoints are yours to move — a short day is inserted by placing a waypoint where the short day should end.
Does it estimate walking time too?
The day split is distance-based; per-leg times with climb belong to the Hiking Route Planner with Elevation, whose Naismith estimates pair with this document.
Can I print just one day?
Print the book and carry the day you need — paper tears politely along the plan's own seams.
What if a day ends nowhere near a village?
The roadbook names the nearest place; where the trail is empty, that is the warning to carry camping gear, printed in advance.
Days of different lengths for strong and weak legs?
Move a waypoint: the split re-forms around it. The document serves the walkers, not the other way round.
